Abstract:
The adoption of additive manufacturing (AM) has driven extensive research into metal feedstocks, uncovering strong links between powder quality and the performance of printed parts. Poor powder characteristics, inadequate flowability or inconsistent packing, can significantly degrade the mechanical performance of the final 3D-printed components. This study investigates the effects of arc manipulator angle, electrical current, and vibration amplitude on AlSi12 powder quality via ultrasonic atomization (UA). Parameter adjustments significantly influenced particle size distribution, with span variations up to 37.5%. Optimal rheological properties were achieved by increasing the vibration amplitude (from 75 to 80%), decreasing the arc angle (from 5° to -5°), and reducing the current (from 150 A to 140 A). A modified AM suitability factor (AMS) was developed, incorporating logarithmic transformation and custom weighting to mitigate high-uncertainty parameter effects. Results revealed a non-linear relationship between powder suitability and arc angle, with a sharp worsening above 0°. Electrical current had the greatest impact on powder quality, followed by arc angle and vibration amplitude. Benchmarking showed that UA powder achieved suitability factors 21% higher than commercial powder, with improved sphericity compared to the irregular, fused particles of commercial alternatives. These findings underscore the potential of UA to enhance AM part reliability.

Abstract:
Al-Sn binary system is a miscibility gap alloy consisting of an Al-rich phase and a Sn-rich phase. This system is traditionally applied in bearings and more recently found application as form-stable phase change material (PCM) exploiting solid-liquid phase transition of Sn. A careful choice of production process is required to avoid macro-segregation of the two phases, which have different densities and melting temperatures. In the present study, the additive manufacturing process known as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) was applied to an Al-Sn alloy with 20% volume of Sn, as a rapid solidification process. The effect of process parameters on microstructure and hardness was evaluated. Moreover, feasibility and stability with thermal cycles of a lattice structure of the same alloy were experimentally investigated. An Al-Sn lattice structure could be used as container for a lower melting organic PCM (e.g., a paraffin or a fatty acid), providing high thermal diffusivity thanks to the metallic network and a “safety system” reducing thermal diffusivity if the system temperature overcomes Sn melting temperature. Even if focused on Al-Sn to be applied in thermal management systems, the study offers a contribution in view of the optimization of manufacturing processes locally involving high solidification rates and reheat cycles in other miscibility gap alloys (e.g., Fe-Cu) with similar thermal or structural applications.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Al–15Sn–5Pb (vol.%) alloy was fabricated by the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) method at laser scanning speeds of 0.8, 1.0, and 1.2 m/s and laser powers ranging from 70 to 130 W. The samples were synthesized from a mixture of elemental powders using an ONSINT AM150 3D printer under a flowing argon atmosphere. The structure and mechanical properties under compression tests of the produced material were investigated as a function of the volumetric laser energy density (E) during LPBF. It has been established that low laser energy density during LPBF results in incomplete melting of aluminum particles and a non-uniform distribution of soft inclusions within the material. Increasing the energy density ensures a significantly more uniform distribution of the phases, resulting in the formation of a fine-grained three-phase alloy. It was established that both the ductility and strength of the alloy improve with the increase in E until a critical value is reached. As a result, at E ≥ 48 J·mm−3, the ultimate strength of the alloy reaches 100 ± 5 MPa, and its deformation before fracture is 15 ± 1%. Substituting one quarter of the tin volume with lead results in a significant increase in the ductility of the LPBF-fabricated aluminum alloy.</jats:p>

<jats:p>The work studied the effect of high-temperature annealing on the phase composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties of an AlSn10Pb10 vol.% alloy obtained by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). For this purpose, a series of anneals was carried out in the temperature range of 200–500 °C with a duration of 30 min. Using X-ray diffraction, it was determined that the annealed samples had a three-phase structure consisting of Al, β-Sn, and α-Pb phases, with a gradual decrease in their lattice elastic strain and dislocation density as the heating temperature increased. Analysis of the obtained SEM images revealed that these changes were accompanied by the coarsening of Sn and Pb inclusions and growth of the pure aluminum areas. As a result of the described structural changes with increasing annealing temperature, the ultimate compressive strength of the alloy monotonically decreased from 108 MPa (in the as-built state) to 75 MPa after annealing at 500 °C. The alloy’s ductility (strain at peak stress) also improved and reached a maximum of 26% after annealing at 400 °C. Compression test results showed that the optimal combination of ductility and strength of the LPBF-processed AlSn10Pb10 alloy was observed after annealing at 400 °C.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) of titanium alloys enables the production of complex, high-performance components, but the steep thermal gradients and rapid solidification involved make it challenging to control crystallographic texture and phase evolution. This review synthesizes the current understanding of how these thermal conditions influence grain morphology, texture intensity, and solid-state transformations in key alloys such as Ti-6Al-4V (Ti64), Ti-6Al-2Sn-4Zr-2Mo (Ti6242), Ti-5Al-5Mo-5V-3Cr (Ti5553), and metastable β-Ti systems processed by powder bed fusion-based processes (PBF) such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and electron beam powder bed fusion (EBPBF/EBM). Emphasis is placed on mechanisms governing epitaxial columnar β-grain growth, α′ martensite formation, and the development of heterogeneous α/β distributions. The impact of processing variables on texture development and transformation kinetics is critically examined, alongside phase fractions. Across studies, AM-induced textures are consistently linked to mechanical anisotropy, with performance strongly dependent on build direction and alloy chemistry. Post-processing strategies, including tailored heat treatments and hot isostatic pressing (HIP), show clear potential to modify grain structure, reduce texture intensity, and stabilize desirable phase balances in titanium alloys. These insights highlight the emerging ability to deliberately engineer microstructures for reliable, application-specific properties in powder-based AM titanium alloys.</jats:p>

The excerpt identifies several alloying-element interactions that constrain aluminum-alloy design. Lithium strongly affects alloy density and stiffness, while its interaction with copper creates the principal hardening system in Al-Cu-Li alloys. The key ternary strengthening phases are T1 (Al2CuLi), T2 (Al6CuLi3), and TB (Al15Cu8Li3); the dominant precipitate depends on lithium content, with θ′/θ favored at low Li, T1 at intermediate Li, and δ′ at higher Li. Magnesium contributes solid-solution strengthening, but in Al-Cu alloys additions above 1.6 wt.% promote metastable, incoherent S′ (Al2CuMg) near grain boundaries. Silver together with Mg promotes a fine, uniform T1 dispersion, although Ag increases material cost. Manganese interacts with Al-Cu chemistry by forming Al20Cu2Mn3 precipitates that influence grain size, texture, creep resistance, and damage tolerance. Titanium forms Al3Ti and can refine grains; in WAAM, Ti additions provide heterogeneous nucleation sites and promote columnar-to-equiaxed grain transformation, though excessive Ti can produce detrimental Al3Ti volumes. Silicon and magnesium interact to form nanometric solute clusters within the supersaturated α-Al matrix during rapid solidification. These Si-Mg clusters obstruct dislocation motion, increasing strength and strain hardening in the as-built condition. Thermal treatment can coarsen the clusters and reduce these benefits, so processing and heat-treatment conditions must be carefully controlled. Copper also interacts strongly with the Al-Si-Mg system: its solubility is high at elevated temperature, but it precipitates during cooling as Cu-containing intermetallic phases, especially θ (Al2Cu). The precipitation sequence proceeds through GP zones, θ'' and θ', and finally stable θ, with the coherent or semi-coherent early phases providing the greatest strengthening. Copper-containing intermetallics improve hardness, strength, and thermal stability by impeding dislocation movement.                                    2.1. Deep Insight into Developing Novel Compositions Tailored for PBF-LB/M

                             Although the excellent strength-to-weight ratio of Al-based alloys has attracted broad
                                interest in several industrial ﬁelds, their considerable solidiﬁcation shrinkage, tendency to
                              oxidation, high laser reﬂectivity and poor powder ﬂowability make these alloys challenging
                             to process by PBF-LB/M [6,7]. To overcome these common drawbacks of Al-based alloy
                          processed through PBF-LB/M, much effort has been dedicated to ﬁnding novel tailored
                          Al-based compositions characterised by high heat stability and mechanical performance.
                        However, optimising the composition requires an exhaustive trial and error experimen-
                              tation that implies signiﬁcant time and costs. For this reason, developing analytical and
                           computational models for designing and optimising alloy compositions has become one of
                             the most important ongoing challenges in this ﬁeld. As displayed in Figure 2, according to
                             the Scopus database, interest in developing computational models has moved hand in hand
                          with the growth of the PBF-LB/M process. The graph in Figure 2 emphasises, in fact, that
                             as interest in the PBF-LB/M process grew, the need to develop computational models also
                            grew. This synergy in trends can be explained since the ‘trial and error’ approach appeared
                            unsuitable and extremely cost- and time-consuming for this additive technique, while
                           computational models could represent powerful allies in developing new high-performing
                              alloys for the PBF-LB/M process reducing time- and powder-waste.





                              Figure 2. Literature trends on the development of computational models for the novel composition

                         Due to the intrinsic difﬁculty of this task, computer calculations and simulations have
                          been carried out at different length scales, following the integrated computational materials

Summary paragraph

       Additively manufactured (AM) aluminum alloys with high strength and thermal stability

have broad applications in turbine engines, vacuum pumps, heat exchangers, and many other

industrial systems. Employing precipitates with an L12 structure to block dislocation motions is a

widespread strategy to strengthen aluminum. However, to achieve high strength, a high volume

fraction of small precipitates is required, and these characteristics are generally mutually exclusive.

Here, we show that for certain compositions of Al alloys, L12 phases initially precipitate as sub-

micron metastable ternary phases under the rapid solidification conditions of powder bed AM, yet

the subsequent L12 phases that precipitate during heat treatment of the sample remain at the

nanoscale, imparting high strength. For strength to be retained at elevated temperature, these

nanoprecipitates must have low coarsening rates. To inversely design the composition of an alloy

to have these target microstructural features, we used hybrid calculation of phase diagram

(CALPHAD)-based  integrated  computational  materials  engineering (ICME) and Bayesian



                                                                                    1optimization techniques. We tested our approach by designing an Al-Er-Zr-Y-Yb-Ni model alloy,

and the selected composition was manufactured in powder form as AM feedstock. The strength of

specimens manufactured via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) from the designed composition is

comparable to that of wrought Al 7075, yet without cracking that occurs upon LPBF of Al 7075.
After high-temperature (400°C) aging the designed alloy is 50% stronger than the strongest known

benchmark printable Al alloy1. This stable strengthening strategy is applicable to a wide range of

alloys and rapid solidification processes, and our hybrid ML/CALPHAD numerical framework

can be used for the efficient and robust design of alloy microstructures and properties, expanding

the capabilities of additive as well as traditional manufacturing.

Introduction

       Additively manufactured (AM) structural components with complex geometries and

tailored properties at voxel-size resolution will lead to significant leap in performance in various

critical engineering applications. One of the exceptional benefits of AM is that exploiting non-

equilibrium processing pathways, including through  rapid  solidification, can give  rise  to

precipitation of metastable phases1–4, supersaturation of solutes5–7, refining length scales of

microstructural features such as grain and phase size8–13. These microstructural features are

difficult or impossible to develop in slow solidification conditions such as during casting. For

example, metastable phases due to rapid solidification have been reported in Ni, Fe, Ti, Al alloys

and alter their mechanical properties or printability at different length scales2,3,14–20. The features

may also appear in welding, giga casting, and splat quenching when the processing conditions lead

to rapid solidification. Exploiting the rapid solidification may thus unravel new routes for alloy

design.

      Al alloys are the second widest used alloys after steels in industrial applications21. High

(temperature)  strength Al  alloys have been mainly  strengthened with two mechanisms8.

Employing precipitates especially with L12 structures is the first main strategy22. L12 structures

are preferred due to having coherent interfaces to resist coarsening at high temperatures. As the

second strategy, Al grains can be partitioned with eutectic phases to further block dislocation

motions 8. Following the first strategy, strength has an inverse relationship with the precipitate size

based on the Orowan strengthening theory22. Thus, for a given volume fraction of precipitates,

smaller precipitate sizes more effectively block dislocation motions and lead to higher strength.



                                                                                    2Although laser AM processing generally leads to smaller length scales as phases do not have time

to grow due to rapid solidification, precipitate sizes usually grow to the micron scale especially as

the percentage of a desirable precipitate phases increases. Another challenge is that most widely

stability (typically at 250-400°C)8,14,25,26, it is typically necessary to add heavy high melting point

microstructure, we minimized coarsening rates of L12 phases and the percentage of fast-growing

phases (Fig. 2a & Supplementary Fig. S1). To inhibit hot cracking in the sample, we controlled

The excerpt identifies several constraints and limitations of ultrasonic atomization (UA) for aluminum-alloy powder production. UA remains comparatively underexplored and is described as a relatively new technology intended mainly for small- to medium-scale production. Continuous atomization of aluminum melts requires substantial ultrasonic vibration amplitudes because aluminum has low density; rapid oxidation of the droplets is also a specific challenge. Historically, UA was primarily used for materials with low liquidus temperatures, such as solders, although its application has more recently expanded to metals with higher melting points. The cited work reports that more than half of a UA-produced batch can meet additive-manufacturing requirements, indicating that not all produced powder necessarily satisfies those requirements. The excerpt does not provide a maximum processing temperature, a numerical maximum batch size, or measurements of evaporation or loss of volatile alloying elements such as Mn, Zn, Li, or Mg. It therefore cannot establish those values. The provided material also does not quantify how ultrasonic processing affects composition retention, nor does it specify whether volatile-element evaporation is a governing limitation for AlSi12. Those details would need to be obtained from the full article, its experimental methods/results, or other literature specifically studying thermal exposure and alloy chemistry during UA.

The excerpt identifies several process constraints for ultrasonic atomization of aluminum-matrix composite powders. Process efficiency is strongly dependent on the melting heat source: induction and plasma exceeded 40% efficiency, whereas arc melting reached only about 15%. Arc melting is destabilized by the poorly conductive SiC reinforcement, while plasma melting can produce unstable melting, irregular large fragments, scrap, and poor coverage of the sonotrode. For induction melting, increasing the pressure difference from 300 to 500 mbar reduced efficiency from 38% to 26%, and increasing nozzle size from 1.0 to 1.5 mm reduced efficiency from 38% to 19%. Excessive material flow causes large drops to bypass atomization, while nozzle clogging leaves unprocessed material in the crucible, extends processing time, and promotes SiC segregation from AlSiMg. The reinforcement size therefore constrains spout/nozzle selection. Vibration frequency is also important: 40 kHz produced nearly twice the efficiency of 60 kHz because lower frequency permits higher ultrasonic parameters. The excerpt does not report a maximum operating temperature, maximum batch size, or quantitative evaporation/loss of volatile alloying elements such as Mn, Zn, Li, or Mg. Consequently, those values cannot be determined from this source.

lel computations. The parallel expected hypervolume improvement (qEHVI) and parallel noisy
expected hypervolume improvement methods overcome these limitations by enabling the parallel


                                       4calculation of the hypervolume for different points using the inclusion-exclusion principle Daulton
et al. (2020).  Similarly, the parallel parEGO and its noisy variant parallelize the scalarization
process, thereby enabling Bayesian optimization for multi-dimensional problems. Having access
to these acquisition functions for multiobjective optimization, the question naturally arises of how
to select the best algorithm for the application of novel materials design and discovery. Specifically,
there are two important factors to consider:  1.  the surrogate model construction, and 2.  the
acquisition function selection.
   Another challenge in Bayesian Optimization (BO) within materials science is the common
practice of making only a single recommendation per iteration, which is inefficient when multiple
parallel experiments or computations are possible. To address this, several strategies have been
suggested, such as dividing the objective space into clusters based on similarity or distance vectors
to maximize data diversity and informativeness Mamun et al. (2022); Zhan et al. (2021). The
qEHVI also supports the generation of multiple candidate points simultaneously, ensuring proper
propagation of uncertainty.
   This work presents a Bayesian optimization (BO) framework to efficiently optimize multiple
properties simultaneously for Aluminium alloy design problems.  First, we compare the perfor-
mance of two ways of constructing or conditioning the surrogate model on the training data:
maximum likelihood estimation and Monte Carlo simulation. Our analysis shows that maximum
likelihood estimation provides the best trade-off for accuracy and time constraints. Then, we com-
pare three different acquisition functions for 1-dimensional properties optimization, i.e., probability
of improvement (PI), expected improvement (EI), and expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI).
Our results illustrate that all three acquisition functions perform more or less similarly and vastly
outperform the random data acquisition algorithm, with PI being slightly worse than the other
two algorithms. Next, we investigate the performance of four different acquisition functions for
multi-dimensional optimization problems, i.e., expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI), noisy
expected hypervolume improvement (NEHVI), Pareto efficient global optimization (parEGO) and
noisy Pareto efficient global optimization (NparEGO). Except for parEGO, the remaining three


                                       5algorithms outclasses the random data acquisition algorithm. However, when considering the com-
putational cost of computing the utility value with the noisy variant of these algorithms, qEHVI
becomes an automatic choice for multi-dimensional problems; however, for noisy data (e.g., exper-
imental observations), qNEHVI should be preferred to deal with the observation uncertainty. We
also demonstrate that the EHVI can identify the global Pareto front with only a 70-75 evaluation
budget and achieves a hypervolume that is over 90% of the maximum achievable value. Finally, we
demonstrate that multiple data acquisition in each iteration cycle can lead to enhanced performance,
in terms of time to reach a predefined hypervolume, ultimately leading to faster alloy design and
discovery.

METHODS
    In this work, we present an active learning framework for the multi-objective optimization
of Aluminium alloy design and discovery. Below, we briefly describe the underlying theory of
the active learning framework, including surrogate model construction and various single- and
multi-objective acquisition functions.
   Figure 1 illustrates the general workflow of the active learning cycle. The cycle begins with
observed data for ’n’ cases, featuring variables {𝐹1, 𝐹2, ..., 𝐹𝑛} and targets {𝑇1,𝑇2, ...,𝑇𝑛}.  To
simulate a realistic situation, we start with a fixed number of initial points (e.g., 25, 50, etc.)
acquired at random. The initial seed points then undergo a data preparation stage where:

   (a)  For experimental data, data instances where elongation is greater than 60% are removed as
       they might contain experimental measurement errors. Since our objective is to minimize
       the elongation in most of the realistic scenarios, this data processing will have no significant
       impact on the model bias.
   (b) Any feature with null values is removed, and
   (c) The data is scaled between zero and one to remove numerical scale bias.

  A probabilistic model is subsequently trained on these data points, enabling the inference of
data instances where only the feature vector is known. In multi-objective optimization, either a

                                       6single model can be used to model the joint probability distribution of the target properties or
separate models can be trained for each target. Based on the model’s inferences for both single- and
multi-objective problems, the utility value is computed using acquisition functions for the discrete
data instances for which the features are known but the target properties are not. The algorithm
then selects the point or points (in cases where several candidates are chosen in each iteration) that
maximize the utility function. These recommended points are then added to the existing training
database. The cycle continues until it reaches the optimum point. For single-objective optimization,
the minimum or maximum value is considered the optimum and used as the stopping criterion.
For multi-objective optimization, the stopping criterion is the hypervolume covered by the non-
dominated points in the entire database. In situations where the global maximum hypervolume is
not known a priori, the cycle can continue until it reaches a predetermined number of iterations or
a specified hypervolume that meets specific design criteria.
   Based on the above discussion, we can identify two key components in an active learning cycle:

   (a) A probabilistic model, serving as a surrogate model, to approximate the underlying data-
       generating function.  In this article, we use Gaussian processes, which are particularly
        effective in multi-objective optimization.
   (b) An acquisition function is used to quantify the utility of all the candidate data points, which
       then guides the selection of the next data point to evaluate.

Gaussian Process

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Element | Published rapid-solidification / LPBF range (wt.%) and examples | Maximum equilibrium solid solubility in α-Al (wt.%) | Physical ceiling / limiting factor | Recommended lower bound (wt.%) | Recommended upper bound (wt.%) | Lower-bound treatment / confidence |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| Mn | 0–3; AlMn3; Scalmalloy studies report 0.20–0.53; Al–3Ce–0.8Ca–1.9Mn uses 1.88–1.9 (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026) | ≈1.8 at the Al-rich eutectic; direct supporting source not retrieved | Above solubility, Al₆Mn/Al₁₂Mn forms; Mn–Fe–Cr compounds can become coarse “sludge,” although Mn can convert harmful Fe–Si phases to less detrimental α-Al–Fe–Mn–Si morphologies (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000024) | 0 | 2.0 | **Zero control.** Raise to 3 only in a dedicated Al–Mn branch with Fe and Cr constrained. Medium confidence. |
| Cr | 0–3; AlCr3 is reported among LPBF compositions; an Al–Si–Ni–Cr–Fe LPBF alloy contained ≈1.2 Cr (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000050) | ≈0.77; source table reports 0.44 at.% equilibrium and 5–6 at.% under rapid solidification (pqac-00000005) | Low equilibrium solubility; Al₇Cr/Al₁₃Cr₂ and Fe–Mn–Cr sludge become increasingly likely. The 1.2-Cr LPBF alloy was predicted to form Al₁₃Cr₂ (pqac-00000050) | 0 | 1.0 | **Zero control.** A 3% corner is literature-backed but poorly suited to an unconstrained multicomponent box. Medium confidence. |
| Zr | 0–0.42 in Scalmalloy-type powders; examples include 0.13–0.18 in 2xxx/6xxx compositions and 0.08–0.42 in Scalmalloy (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000026) | ≈0.28 at the peritectic; direct supporting source not retrieved | Primary Al₃Zr/Al₃(Sc,Zr) appears above the peritectic or when dissolution is incomplete; a 1300 °C melt ceiling and short holding time make dissolution of concentrated Zr master alloy a practical constraint. | 0 | 0.50 | **Zero control**, but include positive levels ≥0.10 to test grain refinement. Pair with Sc; constrain high Si/Ti because silicides and competing aluminides reduce effective nucleant solute. Medium confidence. |
| Mg | 0–6; Scalmalloy ≈3.02–4.77, AlMg5.7 and AlMg6, and tailored AlSi3.5Mg2.5 have been printed (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000026) | ≈14.9 (18.5 at.%); rapid-solidification extension reported as 36–40 at.% (pqac-00000005) | Practical ceiling is not solubility: Mg evaporation/oxidation, keyhole porosity, composition drift and hot cracking dominate. Mg combines with Si as Mg₂Si (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000027) | 0 | 6.0 | **Zero control.** Record powder-to-build Mg loss. Constrain Mg–Si jointly rather than treating both limits as simultaneously safe. High confidence. |
| Si | 0–20; AlSi7Mg, AlSi10Mg, near-eutectic AlSi12.6 and hypereutectic AlSi16/AlSi20 are reported (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000026) | ≈1.65–1.7; rapid-solidification extension ≈5 at.% (pqac-00000005) | Al–Si eutectic ≈12.6; above it primary Si increasingly forms. Near-eutectic Si narrows the freezing range and suppresses cracking, whereas high-Si corners sacrifice ductility and can contain coarse primary Si (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000026) | 0 | 12.6 | **Zero control.** Use 20 only in a separate hypereutectic branch. {"answer": "# Design-Space Definition for a Bayesian-Optimization LPBF Aluminium-Alloy Campaign

## 1. Introduction and Scope

This document defines per-element composition bounds, physical ceilings, pairwise interaction constraints, total-solute considerations, and impurity tolerances for a 15-element Bayesian-optimization campaign on aluminium-based alloys for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), with powder produced by ultrasonic atomization (UA) of ~100 g charges at ≤1300 °C under argon. The 15 solutes—Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn—are varied independently in wt.% with Al as the balance.

---

## 2. Per-Element Recommendations (a–c)

The following table consolidates published LPBF composition ranges, physical ceilings, and recommended campaign bounds for each element.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Element-by-element commentary

**Silicon (Si):** The most widely used LPBF Al-alloy family is Al-Si, spanning AlSi7Mg through hypereutectic AlSi20 (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000026). The Al-Si eutectic is approximately 12.6 wt.% Si; equilibrium solid solubility is only ~1.65 wt.%, extended to ~5 at.% under rapid solidification (pqac-00000005). Near-eutectic Si compositions narrow the freezing range and suppress hot cracking (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000011). The recommended upper bound of 12.6 wt.% covers the eutectic; hypereutectic compositions (up to 20%) are feasible but should be treated as a separate branch.

**Magnesium (Mg):** Scalmalloy contains 3.02–4.77 wt.% Mg, while AlMg5.7 and AlMg6 have been printed for LPBF (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000026). Equilibrium solubility is very high (~14.9 wt.%), but the practical ceiling is set by evaporation, oxidation, keyhole porosity, and hot cracking rather than solubility (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009). The tailored AlSi3.5Mg2.5 alloy demonstrates intermediate Mg levels in LPBF (pqac-00000002). Recommended range: 0–6 wt.%.

**Copper (Cu):** LPBF 2xxx-series alloys span AlCu2 through AlCu6.8 (pqac-00000026). Equilibrium solubility is ~5.65 wt.% (2.4 at.%), with rapid-solidification extension to 17–18 at.% (pqac-00000005). Cu-rich compositions form Al₂Cu precipitation sequences (GP → θ″ → θ′ → θ) that provide age-hardening (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). However, intermediate Cu levels produce broad freezing ranges and severe hot cracking. Recommended range: 0–6 wt.%, with printability screening above ~4.5%.

**Manganese (Mn):** Scalmalloy contains 0.20–0.53 wt.% Mn, and AlMn3 and Al-3Ce-1.9Mn have been printed (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026). Mn has low equilibrium solubility (~1.8 wt.%) and forms thermally stable Al₆Mn precipitates (pqac-00000024). Mn also beneficially converts harmful Fe-bearing intermetallics to less detrimental α-Al(Fe,Mn)Si morphologies (pqac-00000007). Recommended range: 0–2 wt.%. UA literature notes significant Mn evaporation during atomization (pqac-00000039).

**Chromium (Cr):** AlCr3 is listed among LPBF compositions, and an Al-Si-Ni-Cr-Fe alloy contained ~1.2 wt.% Cr (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000050). Equilibrium solubility is only ~0.77 wt.% (0.44 at.%), though rapid solidification can extend this to 5–6 at.% (pqac-00000005). Above the solubility limit, Al₇Cr and Al₁₃Cr₂ form; combined with Fe and Mn, a "sludge factor" risk arises. Recommended range: 0–1 wt.%.

**Zirconium (Zr):** Scalmalloy contains 0.08–0.42 wt.% Zr, and various 2xxx/6xxx LPBF alloys use 0.13–0.18 wt.% (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000026). The Al-Zr peritectic is at ~0.28 wt.%; above it, primary Al₃Zr can form. The 1300 °C UA ceiling may limit dissolution of concentrated Zr master alloys. Recommended range: 0–0.5 wt.%, with positive levels ≥0.10 to test grain refinement.

**Titanium (Ti):** Used principally as a grain refiner at 0–0.20 wt.% in LPBF alloys (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000026). The Al-Ti peritectic is at ~1.3 wt.%; excess Ti forms coarse primary Al₃Ti. Si can bind Ti in silicides, reducing its grain-refining effectiveness. Recommended range: 0–0.20 wt.%.

**Iron (Fe):** LPBF compositions range from trace levels to AlFe3 (3 wt.%) and rapidly solidified Al-8.5Fe-1.3V-1.7Si (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000026). Equilibrium solubility is extremely low (~0.05 wt.%, 0.025 at.%), with rapid-solidification extension to 4–6 at.% (pqac-00000005). For the Bayesian optimizer, the recommended box constraints (all in wt.%) are:

| Element | Lower | Upper | Notes |
|---------|-------|-------|-------|
| Si | 0 | 12.6 | Zero control; covers eutectic |
| Mg | 0 | 6.0 | Zero control; monitor evaporation |
| Cu | 0 | 6.0 | Zero control; screen for cracking >4.5% |
| Mn | 0 | 2.0 | Zero control |
| Cr | 0 | 1.0 | Zero control |
| Zr | 0 | 0.5 | Zero control; pair with Sc |
| Ti | 0 | 0.2 | Zero control |
| Fe | 0 | 2.0 | Zero control; or hold ≤0.25 as impurity |
| Ni | 0 | 5.0 | Zero control |
| Ce | 0 | 10.0 | Zero control |
| Sc | 0 | 0.8 | Zero control; pair with Zr |
| Li | 0 | 3.0 | Zero control; inert handling required |
| Er | 0 | 1.0 | Zero control; provisional |
| Zn | 0 | 7.0 | Zero control; monitor evaporation |
| Sn | 0 | 10.0 | Zero control; structural campaign |

**Total-solute constraint:** Al ≥ 80 wt.% (total solute ≤ 20 wt.%).

All lower bounds are recommended as zero (true control arms) to enable causal inference about each element's contribution. The optimizer should apply the pairwise constraints in Table 2 as inequality constraints or penalty terms to avoid metallurgically infeasible corners of the design space.

---

## 8. Evidence Gaps

The following areas lack direct LPBF-specific published evidence and rely on established phase-diagram knowledge or provisional estimates:
- Equilibrium solid solubility of Mn, Zr, Ti, Er, Zn, and Sn in Al (standard phase-diagram values were used but not retrieved from the LPBF literature).
- Si suppression of Ti/Zr grain-refining effectiveness under LPBF conditions.
- Mn-Cr-Fe sludge-factor applicability to LPBF (a casting heuristic).
- Complete A20X powder specification.
- Quantitative O and H specifications for commercial LPBF Al-alloy powders.
- Published Al-LPBF Bayesian-optimization campaigns with explicit total-solute caps.
- Er wt.% ranges validated in LPBF experiments (most data are in at.% from computational studies)."}

# Design-Space Definition for a Bayesian-Optimization LPBF Aluminium-Alloy Campaign

## 1. Introduction and Scope

This document defines per-element composition bounds, physical ceilings, pairwise interaction constraints, total-solute considerations, and impurity tolerances for a 15-element Bayesian-optimization campaign on aluminium-based alloys for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), with powder produced by ultrasonic atomization (UA) of ~100 g charges at ≤1300 °C under argon. The 15 solutes—Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn—are varied independently in wt.% with Al as the balance.

---

*Table: Published rapid-solidification ranges, physical ceilings, and recommended Bayesian-optimization bounds for the 15 candidate solutes. Provisional or weakly sourced equilibrium values and recommendations are identified explicitly.*

### Element-by-element commentary

**Silicon (Si):** The most widely used LPBF Al-alloy family is Al-Si, spanning AlSi7Mg through hypereutectic AlSi20 (knoop2020atailoredalsimg pages 1-3, liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15). The Al-Si eutectic is approximately 12.6 wt.% Si; equilibrium solid solubility is only ~1.65 wt.%, extended to ~5 at.% under rapid solidification (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 90-93). Near-eutectic Si compositions narrow the freezing range and suppress hot cracking (aversa2019newaluminumalloys pages 1-3, hyer2021compositiondependentsolidificationcracking pages 2-3). The recommended upper bound of 12.6 wt.% covers the eutectic; hypereutectic compositions (up to 20%) are feasible but should be treated as a separate branch.

**Magnesium (Mg):** Scalmalloy contains 3.02–4.77 wt.% Mg, while AlMg5.7 and AlMg6 have been printed for LPBF (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 2-5, liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15). Equilibrium solubility is very high (~14.9 wt.%), but the practical ceiling is set by evaporation, oxidation, keyhole porosity, and hot cracking rather than solubility (okoro2021irradiationassistedcorrosion pages 22-27, rohilla2024investigationofalcu20si10mga pages 15-17). The tailored AlSi3.5Mg2.5 alloy demonstrates intermediate Mg levels in LPBF (knoop2020atailoredalsimg pages 1-3). Recommended range: 0–6 wt.%.

**Copper (Cu):** LPBF 2xxx-series alloys span AlCu2 through AlCu6.8 (liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15). Equilibrium solubility is ~5.65 wt.% (2.4 at.%), with rapid-solidification extension to 17–18 at.% (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 90-93). Cu-rich compositions form Al₂Cu precipitation sequences (GP → θ″ → θ′ → θ) that provide age-hardening (rohilla2024investigationofalcu20si10mga pages 19-22, rohilla2024investigationofalcu20si10mga pages 15-17). However, intermediate Cu levels produce broad freezing ranges and severe hot cracking. Recommended range: 0–6 wt.%, with printability screening above ~4.5%.

**Manganese (Mn):** Scalmalloy contains 0.20–0.53 wt.% Mn, and AlMn3 and Al-3Ce-1.9Mn have been printed (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 2-5, wei2025compositionoptimizationand pages 2-4, liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15). Mn has low equilibrium solubility (~1.8 wt.%) and forms thermally stable Al₆Mn precipitates (wei2025compositionoptimizationand pages 2-4). Mn also beneficially converts harmful Fe-bearing intermetallics to less detrimental α-Al(Fe,Mn)Si morphologies (okoro2021irradiationassistedcorrosion pages 22-27). Recommended range: 0–2 wt.%. UA literature notes significant Mn evaporation during atomization (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 2-4).

**Chromium (Cr):** AlCr3 is listed among LPBF compositions, and an Al-Si-Ni-Cr-Fe alloy contained ~1.2 wt.% Cr (liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15, cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 132-135). Equilibrium solubility is only ~0.77 wt.% (0.44 at.%), though rapid solidification can extend this to 5–6 at.% (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 90-93). Above the solubility limit, Al₇Cr and Al₁₃Cr₂ form; combined with Fe and Mn, a "sludge factor" risk arises. Recommended range: 0–1 wt.%.

**Zirconium (Zr):** Scalmalloy contains 0.08–0.42 wt.% Zr, and various 2xxx/6xxx LPBF alloys use 0.13–0.18 wt.% (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 2-5, cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 100-103, liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15). The Al-Zr peritectic is at ~0.28 wt.%; above it, primary Al₃Zr can form. The 1300 °C UA ceiling may limit dissolution of concentrated Zr master alloys. Recommended range: 0–0.5 wt.%, with positive levels ≥0.10 to test grain refinement.

**Titanium (Ti):** Used principally as a grain refiner at 0–0.20 wt.% in LPBF alloys (rodriguezgonzalez2023wirearcadditive pages 7-9, liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15). The Al-Ti peritectic is at ~1.3 wt.%; excess Ti forms coarse primary Al₃Ti. Si can bind Ti in silicides, reducing its grain-refining effectiveness. Recommended range: 0–0.20 wt.%.

**Iron (Fe):** LPBF compositions range from trace levels to AlFe3 (3 wt.%) and rapidly solidified Al-8.5Fe-1.3V-1.7Si (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 103-106, liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15). Equilibrium solubility is extremely low (~0.05 wt.%, 0.025 at.%), with rapid-solidification extension to 4–6 at.% (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 90-93). Fe promotes brittle β-AlFeSi plates unless Mn is present to modify morphology (okoro2021irradiationassistedcorrosion pages 22-27, cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 132-135). Recommended range: 0–2 wt.% if Fe is an intentional variable; otherwise ≤0.15–0.25 wt.% as an impurity.

**Nickel (Ni):** LPBF Al-Si-Ni alloys used ~5.1 wt.% Ni, near the ternary Al-Si-Ni eutectic (~4.9 Ni, 10.98 Si at 567 °C) (cattano2019feasibilitystudiesona pages 113-117, cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 113-117). Equilibrium solubility is negligible (~0.05 wt.%), but rapid solidification can extend it to 1.2–7.7 at.% (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 90-93). Al₃Ni forms readily; incomplete dissolution gives coarse Ni-rich agglomerates (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 132-135, cattano2019feasibilitystudiesona pages 126-132). Recommended range: 0–5 wt.%.

**Cerium (Ce):** Binary LPBF Al-10Ce has been printed crack-free; the eutectic is estimated at 10–12 wt.% Ce with a melting point of ~640 °C (hesselmann2022effectofprecipitationforming pages 1-3, liu2024reviewoflaser pages 2-4). Ce solubility in Al is negligible (~0.005–0.01 wt.% at RT) (liu2024reviewoflaser pages 2-4). Al₁₁Ce₃ eutectic structures provide thermal stability. Recommended range: 0–10 wt.%.

**Scandium (Sc):** Scalmalloy powders contain 0.20–0.71 wt.% Sc (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 2-5, aversa2019newaluminumalloys pages 8-10, cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 100-103). Equilibrium solubility is ~0.35–0.4 wt.%, with the Al-Sc eutectic at ~0.55 wt.%; rapid solidification at LPBF cooling rates (10⁴–10⁶ K/s) can retain up to ~3 wt.% Sc in supersaturated solid solution (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 90-93, cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 2-5). Primary Al₃(Sc,Zr) seed crystals nucleate equiaxed grains at melt-pool boundaries (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 2-5). Recommended range: 0–0.80 wt.%.

**Lithium (Li):** LPBF Al-Cu-Li-Mg-Ag-Sc-Zr alloys have been produced with 1, 2, and 3 wt.% Li, and a binary Al-3.2Li has also been printed (shao2024microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2, ji2025influenceoflaser pages 2-4). Equilibrium solubility is 4.2 wt.% (shao2024microstructureandmechanical pages 12-14, shao2024microstructureandmechanical pages 14-15). The practical ceiling is set by preferential evaporation (~15% relative Li loss during SLM) and oxidation rather than solubility (shao2024microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). The 3 wt.% Li alloy achieved only ~92% densification (shao2024microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). Recommended range: 0–3 wt.%, with dedicated inert-atmosphere protocols.

**Erbium (Er):** Al-Er-Zr-Y-Yb-Ni alloys have been designed via hybrid ML/CALPHAD for LPBF; one control composition used ~0.4 at.% Er with ~1 at.% Zr (taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 40-54, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 1-4). Er has very low equilibrium solubility (~0.04–0.05 wt.%) and forms Al₃Er precipitates. Recommended range: 0–1 wt.% (provisional; direct wt.% LPBF evidence is sparse).

**Zinc (Zn):** LPBF 7xxx alloys contain 5.4–6.52 wt.% Zn, and Al-6Zn-2Mg has been reported (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 103-106, cattano2019feasibilitystudiesona pages 103-106, liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15). Zn has very high equilibrium solubility (~80 wt.% near the eutectic), so the practical ceiling is evaporation, composition drift, and hot cracking rather than solubility (cattano2019feasibilitystudiesona pages 103-106). Recommended range: 0–7 wt.%, with chemistry verification pre- and post-atomization.

**Tin (Sn):** LPBF Al-Sn miscibility-gap alloys have been produced at 20 vol.% Sn (~40 wt.% Sn) for bearing/phase-change applications (rusin2025effectoflaser pages 1-2, confalonieri2022effectofprocess pages 1-2, confalonieri2022effectofprocess pages 2-4). Sn is essentially insoluble in solid Al (~0.06 wt.%). At high levels, segregation and weak interfaces limit structural properties. Recommended range: 0–10 wt.% for a structural campaign; a separate Sn-rich branch (up to ~40 wt.%) may be created for functional applications.

---

## 3. Pairwise Interaction Constraints (d)

The following table identifies the key pairwise and multi-element interactions that should constrain the box design space.

| Element pair | Interaction type | Constraint recommendation | Evidence source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Si + Mg | Precipitation / stoichiometric coupling: Mg₂Si forms; rapid solidification also produces Si–Mg clusters. | Do not permit the independent maxima simultaneously without CALPHAD/Scheil screening. Track the Mg₂Si stoichiometric balance: Mg/Si ≈ 1.73 by weight; flag Mg and Si combinations that create excessive eutectic/intermetallic fraction. | Mg₂Si formation and Si–Mg clustering are directly documented (okoro2021irradiationassistedcorrosion pages 22-27, rohilla2024investigationofalcu20si10mga pages 15-17). |
| Si + Ti | Competing silicide formation; Si can reduce the Ti available for Al₃Ti-mediated grain refinement. | At Si >7%, keep Ti approximately ≤0.10–0.15% unless phase calculations or microscopy verify effective grain refinement; avoid the Si and Ti upper bounds together. | No direct supporting evidence was retrieved in the reviewed LPBF sources; treat this as a provisional metallurgical constraint requiring CALPHAD/experimental validation. The surveyed LPBF alloys used Ti only up to about 0.20% (liu2024alloydesignfor pages 14-15). |
| Si + Zr | Competing silicide/intermetallic formation may reduce Zr available for Al₃Zr or Al₃(Sc,Zr). | Avoid combining near-eutectic Si with maximum Zr in the initial campaign; require phase screening when Si >7% and Zr >0.2%. | Direct LPBF evidence that Si consumes Zr was not retrieved. Zr-bearing LPBF alloys generally use ≤0.42% Zr, and Al₃(Sc,Zr) formation is documented (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 2-5, cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 100-103). |
| Si + Fe | Detrimental Fe-bearing intermetallic formation, especially plate/needle-like β-AlFeSi when Mn is insufficient. | For Si-rich alloys, hold Fe ≤0.5%—preferably ≤0.2% for structural alloys—unless Mn is intentionally added and phase morphology is verified. Do not sample high-Si/high-Fe corners by default. | Fe–Si intermetallic formation and Mn modification toward less harmful α-Al–Fe–Mn–Si phases are documented (okoro2021irradiationassistedcorrosion pages 22-27, cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 132-135). |
| Li + Cu | Coupled precipitation: T₁-Al₂CuLi, T₂-Al₆CuLi₃ and Tᴮ-Al₁₅Cu₈Li₃; the dominant phase changes with Li/Cu ratio. | Treat Li and Cu as a coupled subspace. Require CALPHAD/aging-path screening; include designed Li:Cu ratios rather than independent random combinations. Avoid simultaneously maximizing Li and Cu because of evaporation plus hot-cracking risk. | θ/T₁/Tᴮ occurred at 1% Li, T₁/T₂ at 2% Li, and δ′/T₂ at 3% Li; Cu–Li hardening interactions are independently reviewed (rodriguezgonzalez2023wirearcadditive pages 7-9, shao2024microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). |
| Mn + Fe | Intermetallic-morphology modification: Mn can replace Fe and favor α-Al–Fe–Mn–Si rather than harmful Fe–Si phases. | When intentional Fe exceeds approximately 0.3% in a Si-bearing alloy, include an Mn-containing branch; use phase-fraction constraints rather than assuming that more Mn is always beneficial. | Mn was reported to suppress harmful Si–Al–Fe phases by promoting α-Si₂Al₁₅(Fe,Mn)₃ and (Fe,Mn)Al₁₆ (okoro2021irradiationassistedcorrosion pages 22-27). |
| Mn + Cr + Fe | Combined tendency to form dense, coarse Fe–Mn–Cr intermetallic “sludge.” | Use the casting heuristic **SF = Fe + 2Mn + 3Cr <≈1.8** as a conservative pre-screen, not as an LPBF-validated law. ---

## 4. Total-Solute Cap and Campaign Norms (e)

No published high-throughput or Bayesian-optimization LPBF aluminium-alloy campaign was found that specifies an explicit "Al ≥ X%" total-solute constraint. The most relevant BO campaigns are the BIRDSHOT and BRAVE projects on Al-V-Cr-Fe-Co-Ni(-Mn-Cu) high-entropy alloys, which used element-by-element upper bounds (e.g., Al ≤24 at.%, Ni ≤60 at.%) combined with CALPHAD phase-stability filters (FCC stability above 700 °C, solidification range <100 K), rather than a simple total-solute cap (mulukutla2026abravealloy pages 4-5, hastings2024aninteroperablemulti pages 3-5, hastings2024aninteroperablemulti pages 2-3). The Mamun et al. (2025) study applied multi-objective BO (qEHVI) to aluminium alloy optimization but detailed composition bounds were not retrieved from the main text (mamun2025accelerateddevelopmentof pages 1-4, mamun2025accelerateddevelopmentof pages 4-8).

In practice, the vast majority of published LPBF aluminium alloys have Al ≥ 80 wt.% by the nature of the alloy system; the most solute-laden structural examples are Al-10Si-0.3Mg (~89% Al), Scalmalloy (~93.9% Al), and Al-10Ce (~90% Al). Only specialty compositions such as Al-20Si-5Fe-3Cu-1Mg (~71% Al) or Al-40Sn (~60% Al) fall below 80%. **A total-solute cap of Al ≥ 80 wt.% (i.e., ≤20 wt.% total solute) is recommended** as a pragmatic default for structural alloys. This is conservative enough to encompass all major alloy families (Al-Si, Al-Mg-Sc, Al-Cu, Al-Ce, Al-Zn-Mg) while excluding metallurgically impractical extremes. An Al ≥ 75% (25% solute) cap would additionally allow hypereutectic Al-Si and high-Sn compositions, which may be appropriate for specific functional applications.

---

### Key findings:

**AlSi10Mg** is the best-documented LPBF powder. Measured compositions include 10.7 wt.% Si, 0.48 wt.% Mg, 0.19 wt.% Fe, and 0.01 wt.% Ti (cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 126-132). The Fe tolerance of ≤0.55 wt.% is relatively generous because the near-eutectic Si content can accommodate Fe-bearing intermetallics.

**Scalmalloy** powders show Fe 0.01–0.13 wt.% and Si 0.01–0.06 wt.%, which are far tighter than AlSi10Mg, reflecting the sensitivity of Al-Mg-Sc alloys to Fe and Si impurities (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 2-5).

**Master-alloy base selection:** Using 99.7% commercial-purity Al as the base introduces ~0.2% Fe and ~0.1% Si as background impurities. This is acceptable for Si-rich alloys (where Fe ≤0.55% is tolerated) but may be problematic for alloy corners where Fe and Si are both intentionally near zero (e.g., Al-Ce or Al-Mg-Sc compositions). For these cases, 99.99% high-purity Al (Fe+Si < 0.01%) is preferable, though more expensive. A practical compromise is to use 99.7% Al when Si ≥ 3% (since Si is already high) and 99.99% Al when Si < 1% and Fe must be ≤0.15%.

**Oxygen:** LPBF Al-alloy powder oxygen content is typically 200–800 ppm and increases with recycling and handling. One Al-Li alloy powder was reported at 1500 ppm O (ji2025influenceoflaser pages 2-4). UA under argon with induction melting should target <500 ppm O in fresh powder, verified by inert-gas fusion analysis for every batch.

**Hydrogen:** No retrieved source specified a commercial LPBF Al-powder H tolerance, but the casting industry standard of <0.1 mL/100g (equivalent to ~1 ppm by weight) is widely applied. UA under dry argon is expected to keep H well below this threshold.

---

## 6. Ultrasonic Atomization Constraints

UA with induction melting under argon at a ~1300 °C ceiling is compatible with all common aluminium alloy compositions, since the Al liquidus is ~660 °C and most binary eutectics are below 700 °C. The optimal atomization temperature is 1.3–1.5× the absolute melting temperature (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 2-4), which for pure Al corresponds to ~940–1130 °C; the 1300 °C ceiling provides adequate superheat for most alloys. Key UA-specific considerations include:

- **Volatile element loss:** UA literature reports significant Mn and Zn evaporation, especially in the finest powder fractions (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 2-4). Li and Mg are also expected to suffer evaporation losses. Pre- and post-atomization chemical analysis is essential for all batches, particularly those containing Li, Zn, Mg, or Mn.
- **Batch size:** ~100 g charges are standard for lab-scale UA, which is appropriate for the described campaign.
- **Efficiency:** Induction melting provides the highest UA efficiency (~50% usable powder) compared to arc or plasma sources (jedynak2024processabilityofaluminummatrix pages 3-6).
- **High-melting elements:** Zr (melting point 1855 °C), Cr (1907 °C), and Ti (1668 °C) must be supplied as pre-dissolved master alloys (e.g., Al-10Zr, Al-10Cr, Al-10Ti) rather than pure metals, to ensure dissolution at ≤1300 °C.

---

## 7. Summary of Recommended Bounds

For the Bayesian optimizer, the recommended box constraints (all in wt.%) are:

| Element | Lower | Upper | Notes |
|---------|-------|-------|-------|
| Si | 0 | 12.6 | Zero control; covers eutectic |
| Mg | 0 | 6.0 | Zero control; monitor evaporation |
| Cu | 0 | 6.0 | Zero control; screen for cracking >4.5% |
| Mn | 0 | 2.0 | Zero control |
| Cr | 0 | 1.0 | Zero control |
| Zr | 0 | 0.5 | Zero control; pair with Sc |
| Ti | 0 | 0.2 | Zero control |
| Fe | 0 | 2.0 | Zero control; or hold ≤0.25 as impurity |
| Ni | 0 | 5.0 | Zero control |
| Ce | 0 | 10.0 | Zero control |
| Sc | 0 | 0.8 | Zero control; pair with Zr |
| Li | 0 | 3.0 | Zero control; inert handling required |
| Er | 0 | 1.0 | Zero control; provisional |
| Zn | 0 | 7.0 | Zero control; monitor evaporation |
| Sn | 0 | 10.0 | Zero control; structural campaign |

**Total-solute constraint:** Al ≥ 80 wt.% (total solute ≤ 20 wt.%).

All lower bounds are recommended as zero (true control arms) to enable causal inference about each element's contribution. The optimizer should apply the pairwise constraints in Table 2 as inequality constraints or penalty terms to avoid metallurgically infeasible corners of the design space.

---

## 8. Evidence Gaps

The following areas lack direct LPBF-specific published evidence and rely on established phase-diagram knowledge or provisional estimates:
- Equilibrium solid solubility of Mn, Zr, Ti, Er, Zn, and Sn in Al (standard phase-diagram values were used but not retrieved from the LPBF literature).
- Si suppression of Ti/Zr grain-refining effectiveness under LPBF conditions.
- Mn-Cr-Fe sludge-factor applicability to LPBF (a casting heuristic).
- Complete A20X powder specification.
- Quantitative O and H specifications for commercial LPBF Al-alloy powders.
- Published Al-LPBF Bayesian-optimization campaigns with explicit total-solute caps.
- Er wt.% ranges validated in LPBF experiments (most data are in at.% from computational studies).

### Element-by-element commentary

**Silicon (Si):** The most widely used LPBF Al-alloy family is Al-Si, spanning AlSi7Mg through hypereutectic AlSi20 (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000026). The Al-Si eutectic is approximately 12.6 wt.% Si; equilibrium solid solubility is only ~1.65 wt.%, extended to ~5 at.% under rapid solidification (pqac-00000005). Near-eutectic Si compositions narrow the freezing range and suppress hot cracking (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000011). The recommended upper bound of 12.6 wt.% covers the eutectic; hypereutectic compositions (up to 20%) are feasible but should be treated as a separate branch.

**Magnesium (Mg):** Scalmalloy contains 3.02–4.77 wt.% Mg, while AlMg5.7 and AlMg6 have been printed for LPBF (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000026). Equilibrium solubility is very high (~14.9 wt.%), but the practical ceiling is set by evaporation, oxidation, keyhole porosity, and hot cracking rather than solubility (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009). The tailored AlSi3.5Mg2.5 alloy demonstrates intermediate Mg levels in LPBF (pqac-00000002). Recommended range: 0–6 wt.%.

**Copper (Cu):** LPBF 2xxx-series alloys span AlCu2 through AlCu6.8 (pqac-00000026). Equilibrium solubility is ~5.65 wt.% (2.4 at.%), with rapid-solidification extension to 17–18 at.% (pqac-00000005). Cu-rich compositions form Al₂Cu precipitation sequences (GP → θ″ → θ′ → θ) that provide age-hardening (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). However, intermediate Cu levels produce broad freezing ranges and severe hot cracking. Recommended range: 0–6 wt.%, with printability screening above ~4.5%.

**Manganese (Mn):** Scalmalloy contains 0.20–0.53 wt.% Mn, and AlMn3 and Al-3Ce-1.9Mn have been printed (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026). Mn has low equilibrium solubility (~1.8 wt.%) and forms thermally stable Al₆Mn precipitates (pqac-00000024). Mn also beneficially converts harmful Fe-bearing intermetallics to less detrimental α-Al(Fe,Mn)Si morphologies (pqac-00000007). Recommended range: 0–2 wt.%. UA literature notes significant Mn evaporation during atomization (pqac-00000039).

**Chromium (Cr):** AlCr3 is listed among LPBF compositions, and an Al-Si-Ni-Cr-Fe alloy contained ~1.2 wt.% Cr (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000050). Equilibrium solubility is only ~0.77 wt.% (0.44 at.%), though rapid solidification can extend this to 5–6 at.% (pqac-00000005). Above the solubility limit, Al₇Cr and Al₁₃Cr₂ form; combined with Fe and Mn, a "sludge factor" risk arises. Recommended range: 0–1 wt.%.

**Zirconium (Zr):** Scalmalloy contains 0.08–0.42 wt.% Zr, and various 2xxx/6xxx LPBF alloys use 0.13–0.18 wt.% (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000026). The Al-Zr peritectic is at ~0.28 wt.%; above it, primary Al₃Zr can form. The 1300 °C UA ceiling may limit dissolution of concentrated Zr master alloys. Recommended range: 0–0.5 wt.%, with positive levels ≥0.10 to test grain refinement.

**Titanium (Ti):** Used principally as a grain refiner at 0–0.20 wt.% in LPBF alloys (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000026). The Al-Ti peritectic is at ~1.3 wt.%; excess Ti forms coarse primary Al₃Ti. Si can bind Ti in silicides, reducing its grain-refining effectiveness. Recommended range: 0–0.20 wt.%.

**Iron (Fe):** LPBF compositions range from trace levels to AlFe3 (3 wt.%) and rapidly solidified Al-8.5Fe-1.3V-1.7Si (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000026). Equilibrium solubility is extremely low (~0.05 wt.%, 0.025 at.%), with rapid-solidification extension to 4–6 at.% (pqac-00000005). Fe promotes brittle β-AlFeSi plates unless Mn is present to modify morphology (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000050). Recommended range: 0–2 wt.% if Fe is an intentional variable; otherwise ≤0.15–0.25 wt.% as an impurity.

**Nickel (Ni):** LPBF Al-Si-Ni alloys used ~5.1 wt.% Ni, near the ternary Al-Si-Ni eutectic (~4.9 Ni, 10.98 Si at 567 °C) (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000052). Equilibrium solubility is negligible (~0.05 wt.%), but rapid solidification can extend it to 1.2–7.7 at.% (pqac-00000005). Al₃Ni forms readily; incomplete dissolution gives coarse Ni-rich agglomerates (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000053). Recommended range: 0–5 wt.%.

**Cerium (Ce):** Binary LPBF Al-10Ce has been printed crack-free; the eutectic is estimated at 10–12 wt.% Ce with a melting point of ~640 °C (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000013). Ce solubility in Al is negligible (~0.005–0.01 wt.% at RT) (pqac-00000013). Al₁₁Ce₃ eutectic structures provide thermal stability. Recommended range: 0–10 wt.%.

**Scandium (Sc):** Scalmalloy powders contain 0.20–0.71 wt.% Sc (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). Equilibrium solubility is ~0.35–0.4 wt.%, with the Al-Sc eutectic at ~0.55 wt.%; rapid solidification at LPBF cooling rates (10⁴–10⁶ K/s) can retain up to ~3 wt.% Sc in supersaturated solid solution (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012). Primary Al₃(Sc,Zr) seed crystals nucleate equiaxed grains at melt-pool boundaries (pqac-00000012). Recommended range: 0–0.80 wt.%.

**Lithium (Li):** LPBF Al-Cu-Li-Mg-Ag-Sc-Zr alloys have been produced with 1, 2, and 3 wt.% Li, and a binary Al-3.2Li has also been printed (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022). Equilibrium solubility is 4.2 wt.% (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021). The practical ceiling is set by preferential evaporation (~15% relative Li loss during SLM) and oxidation rather than solubility (pqac-00000020). The 3 wt.% Li alloy achieved only ~92% densification (pqac-00000020). Recommended range: 0–3 wt.%, with dedicated inert-atmosphere protocols.

**Erbium (Er):** Al-Er-Zr-Y-Yb-Ni alloys have been designed via hybrid ML/CALPHAD for LPBF; one control composition used ~0.4 at.% Er with ~1 at.% Zr (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029). Er has very low equilibrium solubility (~0.04–0.05 wt.%) and forms Al₃Er precipitates. Recommended range: 0–1 wt.% (provisional; direct wt.% LPBF evidence is sparse).

**Zinc (Zn):** LPBF 7xxx alloys contain 5.4–6.52 wt.% Zn, and Al-6Zn-2Mg has been reported (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). Zn has very high equilibrium solubility (~80 wt.% near the eutectic), so the practical ceiling is evaporation, composition drift, and hot cracking rather than solubility (pqac-00000025). Recommended range: 0–7 wt.%, with chemistry verification pre- and post-atomization.

**Tin (Sn):** LPBF Al-Sn miscibility-gap alloys have been produced at 20 vol.% Sn (~40 wt.% Sn) for bearing/phase-change applications (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000034). Sn is essentially insoluble in solid Al (~0.06 wt.%). At high levels, segregation and weak interfaces limit structural properties. Recommended range: 0–10 wt.% for a structural campaign; a separate Sn-rich branch (up to ~40 wt.%) may be created for functional applications.

---

## 3. Pairwise Interaction Constraints (d)

The following table identifies the key pairwise and multi-element interactions that should constrain the box design space.

| Element pair | Interaction type | Constraint recommendation | Evidence source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Si + Mg | Precipitation / stoichiometric coupling: Mg₂Si forms; rapid solidification also produces Si–Mg clusters. | Do not permit the independent maxima simultaneously without CALPHAD/Scheil screening. Track the Mg₂Si stoichiometric balance: Mg/Si ≈ 1.73 by weight; flag Mg and Si combinations that create excessive eutectic/intermetallic fraction. | Mg₂Si formation and Si–Mg clustering are directly documented (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009). |
| Si + Ti | Competing silicide formation; Si can reduce the Ti available for Al₃Ti-mediated grain refinement. | At Si >7%, keep Ti approximately ≤0.10–0.15% unless phase calculations or microscopy verify effective grain refinement; avoid the Si and Ti upper bounds together. | No direct supporting evidence was retrieved in the reviewed LPBF sources; treat this as a provisional metallurgical constraint requiring CALPHAD/experimental validation. The surveyed LPBF alloys used Ti only up to about 0.20% (pqac-00000026). |
| Si + Zr | Competing silicide/intermetallic formation may reduce Zr available for Al₃Zr or Al₃(Sc,Zr). | Avoid combining near-eutectic Si with maximum Zr in the initial campaign; require phase screening when Si >7% and Zr >0.2%. | Direct LPBF evidence that Si consumes Zr was not retrieved. Zr-bearing LPBF alloys generally use ≤0.42% Zr, and Al₃(Sc,Zr) formation is documented (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015). |
| Si + Fe | Detrimental Fe-bearing intermetallic formation, especially plate/needle-like β-AlFeSi when Mn is insufficient. | For Si-rich alloys, hold Fe ≤0.5%—preferably ≤0.2% for structural alloys—unless Mn is intentionally added and phase morphology is verified. Do not sample high-Si/high-Fe corners by default. | Fe–Si intermetallic formation and Mn modification toward less harmful α-Al–Fe–Mn–Si phases are documented (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000050). |
| Li + Cu | Coupled precipitation: T₁-Al₂CuLi, T₂-Al₆CuLi₃ and Tᴮ-Al₁₅Cu₈Li₃; the dominant phase changes with Li/Cu ratio. | Treat Li and Cu as a coupled subspace. Require CALPHAD/aging-path screening; include designed Li:Cu ratios rather than independent random combinations. Avoid simultaneously maximizing Li and Cu because of evaporation plus hot-cracking risk. | θ/T₁/Tᴮ occurred at 1% Li, T₁/T₂ at 2% Li, and δ′/T₂ at 3% Li; Cu–Li hardening interactions are independently reviewed (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000020). |
| Mn + Fe | Intermetallic-morphology modification: Mn can replace Fe and favor α-Al–Fe–Mn–Si rather than harmful Fe–Si phases. | When intentional Fe exceeds approximately 0.3% in a Si-bearing alloy, include an Mn-containing branch; use phase-fraction constraints rather than assuming that more Mn is always beneficial. | Mn was reported to suppress harmful Si–Al–Fe phases by promoting α-Si₂Al₁₅(Fe,Mn)₃ and (Fe,Mn)Al₁₆ (pqac-00000007). |
| Mn + Cr + Fe | Combined tendency to form dense, coarse Fe–Mn–Cr intermetallic “sludge.” | Use the casting heuristic **SF = Fe + 2Mn + 3Cr <≈1.8** as a conservative pre-screen, not as an LPBF-validated law. Also impose a CALPHAD/Scheil cap on primary intermetallic fraction. | The numerical sludge-factor threshold was not supported by a retrieved LPBF source. LPBF evidence does show Al₁₃Cr₂ and β-AlFeSi formation in a combined Al–Si–Ni–Cr–Fe alloy (pqac-00000050). |
| Zr + Sc | Synergistic nucleation and precipitation: Al₃(Sc,Zr), including co-precipitated/core–shell dispersoids, improves grain refinement and coarsening resistance. | Preserve paired Sc–Zr designs: for example, Sc 0.2–0.8% with Zr 0.1–0.5%. Constrain excessive Sc + Zr that would create coarse primary aluminides; assess master-alloy dissolution under the 1300 °C ceiling. | Scalmalloy contains both additions, and primary/eutectic Al₃(Sc,Zr), supersaturation and precipitation are documented (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000018). |
| Mg + Zn | Volatile-solute coupling plus 7xxx-type broad freezing ranges and cracking susceptibility. | Do not combine Mg 6% with Zn 7% in the unrestricted box. For a 7xxx branch, target approximately Zn 5–7% and Mg 1.5–3%, measure powder/build chemistry, and apply hot-cracking screening. | Published LPBF examples include Al–6Zn–2Mg and AA7050/7075-type compositions; Cu, Mg and Zn broaden the solidification interval (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). |
| Mg + Li | Preferential evaporation/oxidation of both low-boiling alloying elements during melting and LPBF. | Avoid simultaneous maxima; use a dedicated volatile-alloy protocol with late additions, minimal superheat/hold time, inert handling and pre-/post-atomization chemical analysis. | LPBF Al–Li alloys show evaporation of Li and Mg, with approximately 15% relative Li loss reported (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). |
| Zn + Li | Strong combined volatility and oxidation sensitivity; composition can drift during induction melting, atomization and LPBF. | Exclude the high-Zn/high-Li corner initially. If retained, require sealed inert handling and chemistry-based acceptance limits after both atomization and printing. | Zn and Li are identified as high-vapor-pressure elements; ultrasonic atomization literature warns that excessive temperature causes volatile-element loss (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000039). Direct LPBF Al–Zn–Li evidence was not retrieved. |
| Ce + Ni | Eutectic/intermetallic network formation can improve printability and elevated-temperature stability but may create coarse primary compounds. | Explore Ce–Ni only as a designed eutectic branch; keep Ce near 6–10% and begin with Ni ≤2–3%, using Scheil calculations to limit primary Al–Ce/Ni-rich phases. | Al–Ce–Ni is identified as an LPBF alloy-development system; Al–Ce eutectic behavior and Al₃Ni formation are documented separately (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000049). A quantitative Ce–Ni constraint was not retrieved. |
| Ce + Mg | Eutectic plus solid-solution/precipitation strengthening; high Mg adds evaporation and cracking risks. | For a near-eutectic Ce branch, avoid pairing Ce ≈10% with Mg ≈6–10% without phase and volatility screening. A conservative initial branch is Ce 6–10% with Mg 0–4%. | Published Al–Ce–Mg concepts contain approximately 6–10% Mg, and Al–Ce–Mg is identified as an LPBF development system (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000013). |
| Er + Zr | Cooperative L1₂-Al₃M precipitation and coarsening resistance; Zr strongly slows coarsening while Er increases L1₂ phase fraction. | Sample Er and Zr jointly rather than independently: begin near Er 0.1–0.5% and Zr 0.1–0.5%; require phase screening above these levels to prevent coarse primary Al₃(Er,Zr). | Hybrid ML/CALPHAD design of Al–Er–Zr–Ni alloys identified complementary Er and Zr effects and documented an Er–Zr control composition (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029). |


*Table: Pairwise and multielement constraints for screening the nominal composition box before atomization and LPBF. Rows explicitly distinguish directly supported interactions from provisional metallurgical heuristics where LPBF-specific evidence was not retrieved.*

---

## 4. Total-Solute Cap and Campaign Norms (e)

No published high-throughput or Bayesian-optimization LPBF aluminium-alloy campaign was found that specifies an explicit "Al ≥ X%" total-solute constraint. The most relevant BO campaigns are the BIRDSHOT and BRAVE projects on Al-V-Cr-Fe-Co-Ni(-Mn-Cu) high-entropy alloys, which used element-by-element upper bounds (e.g., Al ≤24 at.%, Ni ≤60 at.%) combined with CALPHAD phase-stability filters (FCC stability above 700 °C, solidification range <100 K), rather than a simple total-solute cap (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000047). The Mamun et al. (2025) study applied multi-objective BO (qEHVI) to aluminium alloy optimization but detailed composition bounds were not retrieved from the main text (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000055).

In practice, the vast majority of published LPBF aluminium alloys have Al ≥ 80 wt.% by the nature of the alloy system; the most solute-laden structural examples are Al-10Si-0.3Mg (~89% Al), Scalmalloy (~93.9% Al), and Al-10Ce (~90% Al). Only specialty compositions such as Al-20Si-5Fe-3Cu-1Mg (~71% Al) or Al-40Sn (~60% Al) fall below 80%. **A total-solute cap of Al ≥ 80 wt.% (i.e., ≤20 wt.% total solute) is recommended** as a pragmatic default for structural alloys. This is conservative enough to encompass all major alloy families (Al-Si, Al-Mg-Sc, Al-Cu, Al-Ce, Al-Zn-Mg) while excluding metallurgically impractical extremes. An Al ≥ 75% (25% solute) cap would additionally allow hypereutectic Al-Si and high-Sn compositions, which may be appropriate for specific functional applications.

---

### Key findings:

**AlSi10Mg** is the best-documented LPBF powder. Measured compositions include 10.7 wt.% Si, 0.48 wt.% Mg, 0.19 wt.% Fe, and 0.01 wt.% Ti (pqac-00000051). The Fe tolerance of ≤0.55 wt.% is relatively generous because the near-eutectic Si content can accommodate Fe-bearing intermetallics.

**Scalmalloy** powders show Fe 0.01–0.13 wt.% and Si 0.01–0.06 wt.%, which are far tighter than AlSi10Mg, reflecting the sensitivity of Al-Mg-Sc alloys to Fe and Si impurities (pqac-00000012).

**Master-alloy base selection:** Using 99.7% commercial-purity Al as the base introduces ~0.2% Fe and ~0.1% Si as background impurities. This is acceptable for Si-rich alloys (where Fe ≤0.55% is tolerated) but may be problematic for alloy corners where Fe and Si are both intentionally near zero (e.g., Al-Ce or Al-Mg-Sc compositions). For these cases, 99.99% high-purity Al (Fe+Si < 0.01%) is preferable, though more expensive. A practical compromise is to use 99.7% Al when Si ≥ 3% (since Si is already high) and 99.99% Al when Si < 1% and Fe must be ≤0.15%.

**Oxygen:** LPBF Al-alloy powder oxygen content is typically 200–800 ppm and increases with recycling and handling. One Al-Li alloy powder was reported at 1500 ppm O (pqac-00000022). UA under argon with induction melting should target <500 ppm O in fresh powder, verified by inert-gas fusion analysis for every batch.

**Hydrogen:** No retrieved source specified a commercial LPBF Al-powder H tolerance, but the casting industry standard of <0.1 mL/100g (equivalent to ~1 ppm by weight) is widely applied. UA under dry argon is expected to keep H well below this threshold.

---

## 6. Ultrasonic Atomization Constraints

UA with induction melting under argon at a ~1300 °C ceiling is compatible with all common aluminium alloy compositions, since the Al liquidus is ~660 °C and most binary eutectics are below 700 °C. The optimal atomization temperature is 1.3–1.5× the absolute melting temperature (pqac-00000039), which for pure Al corresponds to ~940–1130 °C; the 1300 °C ceiling provides adequate superheat for most alloys. Key UA-specific considerations include:

- **Volatile element loss:** UA literature reports significant Mn and Zn evaporation, especially in the finest powder fractions (pqac-00000039). Li and Mg are also expected to suffer evaporation losses. Pre- and post-atomization chemical analysis is essential for all batches, particularly those containing Li, Zn, Mg, or Mn.
- **Batch size:** ~100 g charges are standard for lab-scale UA, which is appropriate for the described campaign.
- **Efficiency:** Induction melting provides the highest UA efficiency (~50% usable powder) compared to arc or plasma sources (pqac-00000038).
- **High-melting elements:** Zr (melting point 1855 °C), Cr (1907 °C), and Ti (1668 °C) must be supplied as pre-dissolved master alloys (e.g., Al-10Zr, Al-10Cr, Al-10Ti) rather than pure metals, to ensure dissolution at ≤1300 °C.

---

## 7. Summary of Recommended Bounds

For the Bayesian optimizer, the recommended box constraints (all in wt.%) are:

| Element | Lower | Upper | Notes |
|---------|-------|-------|-------|
| Si | 0 | 12.6 | Zero control; covers eutectic |
| Mg | 0 | 6.0 | Zero control; monitor evaporation |
| Cu | 0 | 6.0 | Zero control; screen for cracking >4.5% |
| Mn | 0 | 2.0 | Zero control |
| Cr | 0 | 1.0 | Zero control |
| Zr | 0 | 0.5 | Zero control; pair with Sc |
| Ti | 0 | 0.2 | Zero control |
| Fe | 0 | 2.0 | Zero control; or hold ≤0.25 as impurity |
| Ni | 0 | 5.0 | Zero control |
| Ce | 0 | 10.0 | Zero control |
| Sc | 0 | 0.8 | Zero control; pair with Zr |
| Li | 0 | 3.0 | Zero control; inert handling required |
| Er | 0 | 1.0 | Zero control; provisional |
| Zn | 0 | 7.0 | Zero control; monitor evaporation |
| Sn | 0 | 10.0 | Zero control; structural campaign |

**Total-solute constraint:** Al ≥ 80 wt.% (total solute ≤ 20 wt.%).

All lower bounds are recommended as zero (true control arms) to enable causal inference about each element's contribution. The optimizer should apply the pairwise constraints in Table 2 as inequality constraints or penalty terms to avoid metallurgically infeasible corners of the design space.

---

## 8. Evidence Gaps

The following areas lack direct LPBF-specific published evidence and rely on established phase-diagram knowledge or provisional estimates:
- Equilibrium solid solubility of Mn, Zr, Ti, Er, Zn, and Sn in Al (standard phase-diagram values were used but not retrieved from the LPBF literature).
- Si suppression of Ti/Zr grain-refining effectiveness under LPBF conditions.
- Mn-Cr-Fe sludge-factor applicability to LPBF (a casting heuristic).
- Complete A20X powder specification.
- Quantitative O and H specifications for commercial LPBF Al-alloy powders.
- Published Al-LPBF Bayesian-optimization campaigns with explicit total-solute caps.
- Er wt.% ranges validated in LPBF experiments (most data are in at.% from computational studies).

contexts.context: The excerpt directly supports several Al-Si-Mg-Cu interactions relevant to aluminum-alloy design. During rapid solidification in laser powder bed fusion, silicon and magnesium form nanometric solute clusters within the supersaturated α-Al matrix. These clusters obstruct dislocation motion and improve strength and strain hardening. Annealing at 300 °C for two hours causes the clusters to coalesce into larger precipitates, reducing their ability to impede dislocations and thereby lowering tensile strength and strain-hardening capacity. Copper has high solubility in aluminum at elevated temperature but precipitates during cooling and aging, ultimately forming intermetallic θ (Al2Cu). The precipitation sequence proceeds through coherent GP zones and θ''/θ' phases before the stable, incoherent θ phase. GP zones and metastable Cu-containing precipitates are especially effective strengthening barriers because dislocations cannot readily cut through them. Quenched-in vacancies promote copper diffusion and rapid GP-zone formation. Thus, Mg-Si clustering and Cu precipitation can enhance hardness and strength, but thermal processing must be controlled to prevent excessive precipitate coarsening. Lithium strongly affects alloy density and stiffness, while its interaction with copper creates the principal hardening system in Al-Cu-Li alloys. The key ternary strengthening phases are T1 (Al2CuLi), T2 (Al6CuLi3), and TB (Al15Cu8Li3); the dominant precipitate depends on lithium content, with θ′/θ favored at low Li, T1 at intermediate Li, and δ′ at higher Li. Magnesium contributes solid-solution strengthening, but in Al-Cu alloys additions above 1.6 wt.% promote metastable, incoherent S′ (Al2CuMg) near grain boundaries. Silver together with Mg promotes a fine, uniform T1 dispersion, although Ag increases material cost. Manganese interacts with Al-Cu chemistry by forming Al20Cu2Mn3 precipitates that influence grain size, texture, creep resistance, and damage tolerance. Titanium forms Al3Ti and can refine grains; in WAAM, Ti additions provide heterogeneous nucleation sites and promote columnar-to-equiaxed grain transformation, though excessive Ti can produce detrimental Al3Ti volumes. The excerpt does not discuss the requested Si–Ti/Zr, Mg2Si, Fe–β-AlFeSi, Mn–Cr–Fe sludge, or Zr–Sc interactions.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several process constraints for ultrasonic atomization, but it does not provide a complete quantitative limit for aluminum alloys. The molten alloy must be heated from approximately 20°C to an optimal atomization temperature of about 1.3–1.5 times its absolute melting temperature. Higher temperatures improve atomization by reducing surface tension and viscosity, increasing output, and reducing droplet size; however, excessive heating can cause evaporation losses of volatile elements in the atomization chamber. Aluminum is specifically noted as a concern because its boiling point is 2470°C. The system must integrate melting and ultrasonic atomization on the sonotrode, since separate or elevated melting arrangements can cause splashing, interrupted atomization, and poor powder quality. Atomization also occurs in an inert-gas atmosphere, with rapid cooling and powder collection. The supplied passage gives no numerical maximum batch size, no measured evaporation rates or composition losses for Mn, Zn, Li, or Mg, and no explicit maximum operating temperature beyond the discussion of aluminum’s boiling point and the preferred 1.3–1.5-times-melting-temperature range. Therefore, those requested values cannot be established from this excerpt alone; they would require experimental data or other sections of the article.
